title: Anthropic has an unusual plan to keep its employees from insider trading
html:
Don Feria/AP Content Services for Anthropic

Ami Vora, Anthropic's chief product officer, and Daniela Amodei, its president.

After its initial public offering set for Thursday, Anthropic will require employees who sell shares to use an unusual structure that aims to counter insider trading, Business Insider has learned.

The arrangement is rare for rank-and-file workers. To sell stock in most cases, Anthropic employees will need to create what's known as a 10b5-1 plan — a written agreement that lists the size of a stock sale, its price, and a sale date at least 30 days in the future.

10b5-1 plans are meant to help companies assure the Securities and Exchange Commission that stock sales don't violate insider trading law. They're mainly used for executives; for most employees, other major tech companies rely on blackout windows that block trades during certain times, which is less restrictive.

Teresa Greenip, a wealth management director at Aspiriant who works with Anthropic employees, said the stock sales setup lets information flow more freely. Executives can share more details about internal finances and other stock-moving information with staff without worrying about those staffers running afoul of insider trading laws, since they're subject to the strict stock trading policy.

The forced discipline will also help workers avoid reactive trading.

"If you wake up and you see a headline, you cannot immediately go and change your stock sales plan," Greenip said.

Greenip said that the 10b5-1 policy will only take effect after Anthropic employees have passed two initial sell-off windows: IPO day, when 10% of employee shares can be sold, and after the company's first quarterly report early next year, when another 35% can go on the block.

After those two windows, employees will need to make their 10b5-1 plans in a five-day trading window around Anthropic's quarterly reports, Greenip said.

The SEC's 10b5-1 rule states that an employee can't set their sale date within 30 days. Greenip says that Anthropic is extending that requirement to 60 days for many employees.

Greenip said companies generally don't enforce this system for all their employees.

"It historically has only been required of those employees who are high-level, in upper management," she said.

Anthropic declined to comment.

Anthropic's IPO is coming up

Anthropic had around 5,300 employees as of the end of September, making it a fraction of the size of the tech companies it can now, at its targeted $1.4 trillion valuation, call peers.

For workers, the shift to public markets can mean a heightened focus on revenue and other metrics that please Wall Street. Brian Boland, a former Facebook executive who worked at the company during its 2012 IPO, told Business Insider that stock price pressure ramped up when employees realized that stock options help them hire talent and acquire companies.

The 10b5-1 policy, Greenip said, should help alleviate some of the pressure from the fluctuations of Anthropic's price. Employees can set target sales prices in their plans, but they cannot sell based on day-to-day reactions.

"Anthropic has encouraged them not to focus on that daily stock price movement," Greenip said.

She added, "Sometimes these exogenous events happen out of your control, and that is what we're stepping into when we move from a private company to a public company."

The Information reported that Anthropic was considering the 10b5-1 policy earlier this year.

summary: Post-IPO, Anthropic employees will need to create what's known as a 10b5-1 plan, a written agreement that fixes stock sales to block insider trading.
